title: 3.1× Review Lift — Restaurant NFC Card Program
summary: A US fast-casual restaurant chain deployed Proud Tek Google Review NFC cards at 412 stores, with one tabletop card per booth and a hand-held card at the takeout counter. Average Google reviews per store / month rose from 14 (control) to 43 (deployment) in the first 90 days — a 3.07× lift. The chain's overall Google rating moved from 4.2 to 4.4 stars chain-wide.

brief.label: Measured results (90-day post-deployment vs control)

sections.title: Why NFC cards (and not QR codes alone)
sections.intro: QR codes work but the friction is higher — the guest must open their camera app, frame the code, tap the link, then write the review. NFC reduces this to a single tap, no camera, no app. In a fast-casual setting where the guest is mid-meal or mid-pickup, the friction reduction is the lever.
bullets: QR code conversion to a posted review: roughly 0.7% of tabletop impressions in the control period.
NFC tap conversion to a posted review: 2.1% of tap events in the deployment period.
Per-card tap rate at tabletop: 5–7 taps / card / day across 412 stores.
Per-card tap rate at takeout counter: 12–18 taps / card / day (higher because the cashier verbally invites the guest).

sections.title: Why NTAG215 specifically
sections.intro: NTAG215 is the workhorse of NFC marketing cards — 504 bytes of user memory is enough for a Google Review URL plus a fallback redirect, the chip is universally readable by every iPhone (since iOS 13) and every NFC-enabled Android (since Android 4.4), and the chip-cost economics work at the customer's volume.
bullets: NTAG213 (180 bytes) — considered, sufficient for the URL alone but no room for a fallback redirect.
NTAG215 (504 bytes) — chosen, room for the URL + the fallback redirect + a tap-counter tag (private chip memory).
NTAG216 (888 bytes) — overkill, ~$0.04 / unit more expensive with no functional benefit for this use case.
NTAG424 DNA — considered for the future programme expansion (authenticated taps for loyalty), not used in this case study.

sections.title: Deployment logistics across 412 stores
sections.intro: Cards needed to be per-store-encoded (each store has a unique Google review URL) and shipped to the store with the artwork matching the chain's brand standards. Proud Tek ran the per-store encoding in Shenzhen using a database of store IDs supplied by the customer's IT team, then shipped one branded card set per store via FedEx ground.
bullets: Per-store encoding at Proud Tek factory using a Mühlbauer encoding line — 8,000 cards / hour throughput.
Master URL pattern — https://g.page/r/<store-id>/review, with <store-id> drawn from the customer's IT team's CSV.
Quality gate — every card read post-encoding to verify the URL matches the store-ID database. 100% test, 0 mis-encoded cards in the deployment lot.
Total production-to-store lead time: 28 days (production 18 days, FedEx 6 days, store-team activation 4 days).

sections.title: Operational results at 90 days post-deployment

items.label: Lift in monthly Google reviews per store

paragraphs: The customer's CX team modelled the Google review programme on a 'review velocity' KPI — reviews per store per month, normalised by transaction volume. The 3.07× lift held steady through month 6 and showed no sign of habituation decay in the year-1 data. The customer expanded the programme to include hand-held cards for shift leaders and is piloting NTAG424 DNA cards as a future authenticated-loyalty card.

sections.title: How the card program was built — chip, encoding, artwork, rollout
sections.intro: A review card only works if the guest never has to think about it, so the build came down to four deliberate choices: a universally-readable chip, a per-store URL burned in at the factory, brand-matched artwork, and a two-placement drop that put a card exactly where the guest's hands already were. The same specification is documented on the [Google Review NFC card solution](/solutions/google-review-nfc-card/) page.
bullets: Chip: NXP NTAG215 — an NFC Forum Type 2 tag with 504 bytes of user memory, room for the Google Review URL plus a fallback redirect, readable by every iPhone since iOS 13 and every NFC-enabled Android since Android 4.4.

Encoding: each card was written with its store's own Google Review URL (https://g.page/r/<store-id>/review) on Proud Tek's Mühlbauer line at 8,000 cards / hour, then 100% read-verified against the store-ID database — 0 mis-encoded cards in the deployment lot.
Form factor: an 85 × 55 mm PVC card, tabletop matte finish with a spot UV brand mark and a QR code fallback printed on the reverse for the few phones without a tap path.

Placement: one card per booth plus one hand-held card at the takeout counter — the counter card sees 12–18 taps a day because the cashier says the words out loud, against 5–7 taps a day on a passive tabletop card.
Rollout: production to store shelf in 28 days (18 days production, 6 days FedEx ground, 4 days store-team activation), shipped as one branded card set per store across all 412 stores.

sections.title: The tap-to-review path — one gesture from booth to posted review
sections.intro: This is the whole product in one gesture. The guest taps the card, the phone opens the store's Google Review URL, and the rating posts — no camera, no app, no typing a search into Maps. Removing those steps is exactly what moved tabletop conversion from 0.7% on a QR code to 2.1% on a tap.

image.alt: Three-step tap-to-review flow: a guest taps their phone to the NTAG215 NFC Forum Type 2 card, the phone opens the store's per-store Google Review URL, and the rating posts to the store's profile, with a QR code fallback on the card reverse; tabletop conversion rose from 0.7% on a QR code to 2.1% on an NFC tap.

bullets: Tap: the guest holds their phone to the NTAG215 card at the booth or takeout counter — NFC Forum Type 2 tags are read natively, with no app to open first.
Open: the phone reads the encoded per-store URL (https://g.page/r/<store-id>/review) and opens it directly in the browser.
Post: the guest lands on the store's own Google review screen and leaves a rating — the single step the card exists to make frictionless.
Fallback: phones without a tap path (older iPhone 7–X, non-NFC Android) use the QR code on the card's reverse, so no guest reaches a dead end.

sections.title: What 90 days changed — reviews, rating, and sentiment
sections.intro: Every figure here is the customer's own measured result over the first 90 days against the pre-deployment control — reported, not modelled. The headline is review velocity: monthly reviews per store went from 14 to 43.

image.alt: Results after the first 90 days versus the pre-deployment control: Google reviews per store per month rose from 14 to 43, a 3.07× lift; the chain-wide rating moved from 4.2 to 4.4 stars; 91% of reviews were 4 or 5 stars versus 84% in the control; and NFC tap-to-review conversion was 2.1% versus 0.7% for QR, across 412 stores.

bullets: Review volume: 14 reviews / store / month in the control period rose to 43 in the first 90 days — a 3.07× lift that held through month 6 with no habituation decay in the year-1 data.
Rating: the chain-wide Google rating moved from 4.2 to 4.4 stars (+0.2 ⭐) as review volume climbed.
Sentiment: 91% of deployment-period reviews were 4 or 5 stars, up from 84% in the control period — the prompt lifted review quality, not just count.
Reach: the program ran across all 412 stores, and the customer has since expanded it to hand-held cards for shift leaders.

sections.title: What transfers — where a tap-to-review card fits next
sections.intro: The mechanics that made this work — a universally-readable NFC tag, a per-location review URL, and a card placed where the customer's hands already are — aren't specific to fast-casual restaurants. The same pattern moves onto any high-footfall, review-sensitive business; the [Google Review cards for restaurants](/solutions/google-review-cards-for-restaurants/) page documents the workflow, and the [Google Review NFC card setup guide](/guides/google-review-nfc-card-setup/) covers the per-store URL encoding end to end.
bullets: Multi-location hospitality — cafés, bars, and quick-service groups where each site has its own Google Business Profile and its own review URL to encode.
Personal-service chains — salons, clinics, gyms, and auto service, where a front-desk hand-off is the natural moment to invite a tap.
Any counter with a verbal prompt — the takeout-counter pattern, where a staff member invites the tap, was the highest-converting placement and transfers to any service desk.

Choosing the chip is the one real decision — the [NTAG213 vs NTAG215 vs NTAG216](/compare/ntag213-vs-ntag215-vs-ntag216/) comparison covers when the extra memory of NTAG215 earns its keep over NTAG213.

faq.question: Does the NFC tap work on every modern smartphone?
faq.answer: Yes. NFC-Forum Type 2 tags (NTAG21x) are read natively by every iPhone since iPhone XS (iOS 13+) without opening any app, and every NFC-enabled Android since Android 4.4. The tap opens the encoded URL directly in the browser. For older iPhones (iPhone 7–X) the user must open the Camera app first; for Android phones without NFC the QR fallback on the reverse of the card handles it.

faq.question: How is per-store encoding handled at scale?
faq.answer: The customer provides a CSV with two columns: store ID and Google Review URL. Proud Tek's Mühlbauer encoding line consumes the CSV and encodes each card in sequence, then prints the matching store ID on a small panel of the card so the store-receiving team can verify the right cards arrived. 100% of cards are read back after encoding to verify URL correctness.

faq.question: What is the lifespan of a tabletop NFC card?
faq.answer: The chip is rated for 100,000 read cycles and 10 years of data retention. The mechanical lifespan is constrained by the PVC body — at the rate of 5–7 taps / card / day a tabletop card shows light wear at 12 months and is typically replaced at 18–24 months. The customer's chain budgets a card replacement every 18 months as a brand-refresh trigger.

faq.question: Can the same card be repurposed for loyalty later?
faq.answer: NTAG215 has a writable user memory but not the cryptographic authentication required for secure loyalty (cloning protection). For an authenticated loyalty card the chip family must be NTAG424 DNA or {chip:nxp-mifare-desfire-ev3:short_name}. The customer is piloting NTAG424 DNA cards as the next-generation card; the current NTAG215 cards will remain the review-prompt SKU.
